introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.summary: Tachyon is a polyglot, file-system-routed full-stack framework distributed through the standalone ty binary. Tac is the frontend layer and Yon is the backend/runtime layer.

sections.heading: Install
sections.body: Tachyon ships as the standalone `ty` binary — no package manager or runtime toolchain required. Scaffold an app and start the development server: Tachyon detects whether a project has a client/, a server/, or both, and serves the right thing on one port. Request validation is performed by CHEX, an external binary the server drives and names through TAC_CHEX_BINARY; identifiers are generated in-process.
sections.code:
curl -fsSL https://tachyon.del.ma/install.sh | sh
ty init my-app --name "My App"
cd my-app
ty preview

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: Pages live in client/pages, components in client/components, and backend routes in server/routes. A companion file sits beside its tac.html template; shared browser assets and data live under client/shared.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/hero/tac.html
  components/hero/tac.js
  shared/assets/  shared/data/
server/
  routes/posts/yon.js

routing.title: Routing
routing.summary: Both layers route from the file system: a directory is a path, and dynamic segments use _slug directories that become :slug parameters at runtime.

sections.heading: Frontend pages
sections.body: client/pages/tac.html serves /, client/pages/docs/tac.html serves /docs, and client/pages/docs/_topic/tac.html serves /docs/:topic — the page you are reading uses exactly that dynamic segment. An ancestor page containing a slot element becomes a reusable shell for its descendants.
sections.code:
client/pages/
  tac.html          -> /
  docs/tac.html     -> /docs (shell with <slot />)
  docs/_topic/
    tac.html        -> /docs/:topic

sections.heading: Backend routes
sections.body: A route file at `server/routes/<path>/yon.<ext>` declares a class with `@Controller` whose static methods are HTTP verbs. The class name ends in `Controller`, and a controller declares HTTP methods and nothing else — the dispatch finds the method by name, so a helper beside GET would never be reached. A route may be split across sibling `yon` files declaring non-overlapping verbs, in any of the eight languages Yon runs.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.body: An `OPTIONS.schema.json` beside each handler declares what a caller sends and receives, with CHEX regular-expression schemas: every value is a pattern and a `?` suffix marks an optional field. The server hands CHEX the declared schema and the request and relays its verdict, rather than re-implementing the schematics and creating a second interpretation of the same file.

yon.title: Yon backend
yon.summary: Yon owns server routes. A route is a directory holding a yon.<ext>; a handler is a class and its HTTP methods, in one of the eight languages that can declare a layer. One bounded process per request, with the protocol supplied rather than written.

sections.heading: Serve modes
sections.body: Tac and Yon are not separate servers and never were: one process builds the client and serves the routes. What a project has decides what it reports on start — "Tac and Yon", "Tac only; no server/routes", or "Yon only; no client/pages". `ty preview` rebuilds when sources change; `ty start` serves what was published and never rebuilds.
sections.code:
ty preview               # development
ty start --port 8080     # serve what was published

sections.heading: Route convention
sections.body: A route is a directory under `server/routes` holding a `yon.<ext>`. A directory beginning with an underscore is a dynamic segment, and it reaches the handler in `parameters` — the same way in every language Yon runs.
sections.code:
server/routes/items/yon.py          ->  /items
server/routes/items/_id/yon.py      ->  /items/:id
server/routes/api/search/_q/yon.js  ->  /api/search/:q

sections.heading: Eight languages
sections.body: Yon runs the languages whose syntax can carry a class annotation: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Kotlin, PHP and Rust. A handler declares its layer with `@Controller`, and a language that cannot make that declaration cannot be a handler — Go, Ruby, Perl, C and C++ are refused with TY2003 naming the supported set, and reached through `@Relay` instead. There is no shebang: Yon knows how to start each of the eight, so a handler declares its methods and nothing about its own execution.
sections.code:
yon.js, yon.ts    a built-in adapter, on a runtime that reads it
yon.py            a built-in adapter
yon.php           php, with the protocol runtime appended
yon.java          JEP 330 single-file source launch
yon.rs            rustc, with a proc-macro crate for the attributes
yon.kt            kotlinc, run with java -jar
yon.cs            a generated project, built with dotnet

sections.heading: What a handler is
sections.body: A class and its HTTP methods. Nothing reads standard input, nothing writes an envelope, and nothing declares a `main` — that half is Tachyon's, appended or compiled beside the file the author wrote. A method the handler does not declare answers 405 without being written. The class carrying `@Controller` is the handler, whatever it is called, and its name must end in `Controller` (TY2011).

sections.heading: Layers
sections.body: A server class declares its layer. Tachyon checks stereotype placement (TY2008) and dependency references (TY2009) at the source-file entry point, plus class names (TY2011) and the controller's own methods (TY2012). Services may use repositories, clients and delegates; those lower layers are peers, not a stack. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and PHP may import separate layer source files. Java, Kotlin, C# and Rust currently prepare one yon source file: place helper types beside the controller in that file rather than importing separate application layer files. The controller's HTTP-only method rule does not prohibit methods on those helper types, but colocated helpers do not acquire independently enforced layer dependency graphs. Java uses source-file launch; Kotlin, C# and Rust have managed compilation steps. This is not dependency injection or a persistent singleton container.

sections.heading: Process lifecycle
sections.body: The default process mode starts one supervised handler process per request. It reads the request, writes its response or bounded stream, then exits. Prepared sources and compiled artifacts use Tachyon-managed content-addressed caching, and execution uses private runtime staging. Cache locations are implementation details, not application-relative paths to import or edit; source, prelude and compilation identity determine reuse. Java remains source-launched rather than an ahead-of-time native executable. The supervisor enforces deadlines, concurrency and frame bounds. Optional isolation drivers are a separate deployment policy.

sections.heading: Route contracts
sections.body: A route may publish an `OPTIONS.schema.json` describing what a caller sends and receives. Every value is a regular expression and a `?` suffix marks an optional field. Validation is performed by CHEX — the server hands it the declared schema and the request, and relays its verdict, rather than re-implementing the schematics and creating a second interpretation of the same file.

sections.heading: Streaming
sections.body: A handler that yields is a stream: each value becomes one server-sent event, and the stream ends when the handler does. `@Stream` on the method is how the route says so before it is called — the server chooses the streaming path before the handler runs, so it cannot wait to see what comes back. The annotation and the body are checked against each other (TY2013), and `@Stream` in a language that cannot stream is refused (TY2014) rather than accepted and quietly ignored.

sections.heading: Relaying to other languages
sections.body: A program Yon does not run is still a program, and one that speaks Handler Protocol v1 on standard input and output is exactly what Yon spawns anyway. `@Relay` on a method makes it a proxy for one. The command sits on the declaration because it is metadata about the method, and it is explicit rather than inferred from the file name — a compiled Go binary and a Ruby script are the same call. A program that cannot be started answers 502 with the reason.

sections.heading: Middleware
sections.body: A `middleware.<ext>` at the project root is consulted before every request and after every response. It answers `before` and `after` rather than an HTTP method, so it speaks the protocol itself: JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and PHP only. The compiled four are not supported, because the protocol runtime appended to a compiled handler dispatches on the method and would find neither.

sections.heading: Isolation
sections.body: `YON_ISOLATION=process` is the default: one directly supervised child process per request. `YON_ISOLATION=firecracker` hands each request to a microVM control program instead, configured by `YON_FIRECRACKER_DRIVER`, `POOL`, `VCPUS`, `MEMORY_MIB` and `EGRESS`. It is read from the environment rather than a config file, because which isolation a deployment wants is a property of where it runs, not of the source — the same build runs either way. An invalid or half-declared policy fails as TY2010 before a handler runs.

sections.heading: Serving
sections.body: `ty start` reads `YON_HOST` (or `YON_HOSTNAME`), `YON_PORT` and `TAC_DIST_PATH`, and selects handler runtimes with `YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME` and `YON_PYTHON_RUNTIME`. The runtime choice matters for more than speed: a `yon.js` or `yon.ts` that declares `@Controller` needs a runtime that transpiles a decorator, so Bun is the default. Overrides must pass the runtime capability probe before startup.
sections.code:
YON_PORT=8080 \
TAC_DIST_PATH=dist/web \
YON_JAVASCRIPT_RUNTIME=$(command -v bun) \
  ty start

sections.heading: JSON in every language
sections.body: Java, Kotlin and Rust have no JSON in their standard libraries, and each compiles as a single file with nowhere to declare a dependency — so Tachyon supplies one, in scope without an import, under the same name in each: `Json.write` and `Json.parse`. C# has one in the box and gets the same name wrapped around it. PHP, JavaScript, TypeScript and Python use their own.

templates.title: Tac templates
templates.summary: Templates are HTML with braces for interpolation, on:event attributes for delegated events, loop, logic, and switch elements for control flow, and explicit island hydration policies.

sections.heading: Interpolation and events
sections.body: Braces evaluate JavaScript inside the async render function, so await is available anywhere. Event handlers are single expressions compiled to one delegated listener per event type, registered at the document and hydrated off the critical path with lossless replay.
sections.code: {headline}

sections.heading: Control flow
sections.body: Loops, conditionals and switches are elements, so structure stays visible in the markup.
sections.code:
{post.title}

Ready.

Working…

Done.

sections.heading: Components
sections.body: A component folder under client/components maps to a hyphenated tag: components/panel/users becomes panel-users. Props pass as attributes, and adding the lazy attribute defers loading until the component scrolls into view.

sections.heading: Hydration schedules
sections.body:
Tac has no server-side rendering mode: the browser renderer owns initial DOM creation and every rerender, and the document a route serves contains no rendered view subtree. So `hydrate` does not say when server HTML is adopted — it says when a component's companion activates.

`load` activates immediately, `idle` waits for the browser to be free, `visible` waits for the viewport, `interaction` waits for the first event, and `never` leaves the component inert. A component that only displays what it was given needs no companion at all.
sections.code: <product-card hydrate="visible" :sku="sku" />

sections.heading: Hydration is a literal
sections.body:
`hydrate` must be one of `load`, `idle`, `visible`, `interaction` or `never`, written as a static literal. It cannot be an expression: the schedule is compiled into the render plan, and a value that is only known at run time would have to be resolved after the moment it was meant to decide.

Properties are ordinary values passed to the component. They are evaluated in the browser like everything else, so nothing about them is written into the served document.

native-rendering.title: Native hosts
native-rendering.summary: A native target embeds the platform's own WebView and loads the application's own bundle, so a desktop or mobile app renders exactly what the browser renders. There is one rendering of an application, not two.

sections.heading: One rendering
sections.body:
`web` is a browser target. Native hosts serve the built application bundle from a restricted local origin inside the platform WebView: WKWebView on macOS and iOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux, and Android WebView. The same DOM, CSS and client runtime render the application; browser-engine differences still require testing on each target.

Matching a platform's look is a choice made in the UI layer, with whichever kit the application already uses. It is not something the framework decides by mapping tags to controls.

sections.heading: One HTML source
sections.body: An application writes `tac.html` once. Control elements — `logic`, `loop`, `switch`, `case` — compile into a render plan; the shared client runtime evaluates that plan and mounts components to create the DOM. Published route documents bootstrap that renderer rather than contain a server-rendered view subtree. Native hosts use the same plan and runtime, not a second platform-widget tree.

sections.heading: The engine is the platform's
sections.body: Tachyon builds and vendors no JavaScript engine. Each host uses the one its platform already ships, which is the same engine backing the WebView it embeds.
sections.code:
macOS, iOS   WKWebView      system WebKit and JavaScriptCore
Linux        WebKitGTK      system WebKit and JavaScriptCore dependencies
Windows      WebView2       requires the WebView2 runtime
Android      WebView        uses the installed system WebView provider

sections.heading: What the host adds
sections.body:
Three things. `data-platform="native"` on the document body, so a page can behave differently without sniffing a user agent. `tachyonWindow`, carrying the window controls the manifest granted and nothing else. And the companion channel, in both directions.

There is no capability vocabulary beyond that, deliberately: a compiled companion reaches its platform's SDK because it was compiled as that language for that target, so a list of verbs in the middle would only ever be the subset Tachyon had implemented.

sections.heading: Companions are compiled in
sections.body: A `tac.swift`, `tac.kt`, `tac.cs` or `tac.rs` beside a page is compiled for a supported target and included in its host; it is not a browser WebAssembly component. Swift and Rust use native compilation, Kotlin uses the Android toolchain, and C# uses the Windows .NET host. Components continue to use JavaScript or TypeScript. Native companion code reaches the platform SDK with the host process's OS permissions. A native-only route without a companion for the requested target fails with TY1010.

sections.heading: What the host does not do
sections.body: There is no managed remote-content surface, no always-on-top or opacity control beyond what the manifest grants, no global shortcut registry and no system tray API. Those were a fixed verb vocabulary compiled into each host, and a fixed vocabulary is a ceiling. An application that needs one of them reaches for it from its companion, in the language of the platform it is running on.

companions.title: Companions
companions.summary: A tac.js or tac.ts file beside a template is instantiated automatically; its fields and methods are visible to the template without wiring.

sections.heading: Reactive fields
sections.body: Fields and methods belong to the companion instance. Template event handlers and signal subscriptions refresh the view after completing; code running outside those paths calls await this.tac.render() when it changes state. Fields prefixed with $ persist to sessionStorage; $$ fields persist to localStorage. Persistence records assignments, not mutations inside an array or object: assign a new value to persist a change.

sections.heading: Decorators
sections.body: Tachyon lowers @publish, @subscribe and @onMount at build time. Put each decorator on its own line above an instance field or method. Signal decorators accept an optional quoted name, not an options object. Subscribed fields receive the retained value on attachment; subscribed methods receive new publications. Stack @onMount with @subscribe to invoke a method at initialization as well.

polyglot.title: Polyglot companions
polyglot.summary: Tac companions are colocated controllers for templates. JavaScript and TypeScript run in the browser on every target; native page companions compile for the platforms their languages support.

sections.heading: Choose a companion language
sections.body: Components use tac.js or tac.ts. A page may additionally provide tac.rs, tac.swift, tac.kt or tac.cs beside tac.html. JavaScript and TypeScript run on every target; native page companions run on their supported targets — Rust on desktop, Swift on Apple, Kotlin on Android, C# on Windows. Provide a JavaScript or TypeScript sibling for web. A native-only route with no companion for the requested target fails with TY1010. Dart and Python are not Tac companion languages.

sections.heading: What a companion reaches
sections.body:
There is no capability vocabulary in the middle. A compiled companion is linked into the host process, so the platform's own SDK is simply there — AppKit, UIKit, the Android framework, the file system — reached because the companion was compiled as that language for that target. A fixed list of verbs in the middle could only ever be the subset Tachyon had got round to implementing, in three hosts, for every platform at once.

What the prelude does supply is the two lifetimes the browser gives a page, spelled the way each language spells a property that persists itself, and one channel back to the page.

sections.heading: Contracts stay on the server
sections.body: OPTIONS.schema.json remains the Yon route contract for incoming requests and outgoing responses. Browser companions call normal HTTP endpoints through this.tac.fetch; native companions may use their platform's networking APIs. Neither declares a second server route protocol.

sections.heading: Where the boundary is
sections.body:
A `tac.js` runs everywhere and reaches browser APIs. A `tac.swift` runs on Apple targets and reaches the platform SDK under the host process's OS permissions. Native companion code is trusted application code, not sandboxed by Tachyon. The page-to-companion bridge is a separate boundary: the host checks the local origin, main frame and canonical route before dispatching supported member operations. Manifest grants still control the exposed window API.

At build time, Tachyon checks language reach: a route whose only companion is a `tac.swift` cannot be built for Android, and TY1010 says so, naming what the route declared.
sections.code:
error[TY1010]: Route '/' has no companion that runs on android.
               It declares Swift (macos, ios).

devices.title: Devices and targets
devices.summary: Tac builds one client source tree into a browser output or a desktop/mobile host embedding the platform WebView. The target selects the output and required platform toolchain, not a second rendering language.

sections.heading: Targets
sections.body: Bundle targets are web, macos, windows, linux, ios and android. web emits browser assets; every non-web target stages a host embedding the platform WebView. Native packaging requires the corresponding SDKs and host tools. The all target expands to every target and writes sibling directories under dist/; it is not a substitute for validating each platform.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target web      # dist/web
ty bundle --target macos    # dist/macos
ty bundle --target windows  # dist/windows
ty bundle --target linux    # dist/linux
ty bundle --target ios      # dist/ios
ty bundle --target android  # dist/android
ty bundle --target all

sections.heading: One bundle, every target
sections.body:
Every non-web target embeds the platform's own WebView and loads the application's own bundle. There is no tag mapping and no fallback boundary to reason about, because there is nothing to fall back from — the bundle renders identically everywhere.

Tachyon used to lower a Tac view into SwiftUI, Compose and WinUI controls and drop into a web view wherever no adapter existed. On a real design almost everything fell back, and what did not looked nothing like the rest. The `--render-mode` flag and `TAC_RENDER_MODE` went with it and are refused if passed.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target macos
ty bundle --target android
ty bundle --target windows

sections.heading: Preview
sections.body: Preview accepts exactly one target. If you omit --target, Tachyon previews web. Native previews check for their platform SDK, compiler and WebView prerequisites, then report missing dependencies before attempting the build.
sections.code:
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos
ty preview --target android

sections.heading: Host context
sections.body: Native hosts mark the document body with data-platform="native". They also expose only the tachyonWindow controls granted by the manifest. There is no this.tac.platform API and no automatic platform, environment, os or target template variable. If a view needs an OS-specific value or capability, declare it in your companion and obtain it through the platform implementation you own.

sections.heading: Rooted terminology
sections.body: platform is the form factor: macos, windows and linux targets are the desktop platform; ios and android are the mobile platform; web is the web platform. environment and os are synonyms for the concrete host: the operating system for native bundles, web for browser bundles. target names the bundle output. Companion language names the language a Tac companion is written in: JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin, Swift or C#.

storage.title: Storage and data
storage.summary: What a browser keeps: fields that outlive a render, responses that outlive a request, and assets that outlive the network. What a server pushes: topics, over server-sent events.

sections.heading: Persisted fields
sections.body: A field prefixed $ persists for the tab and a field prefixed $$ persists across sessions, using sessionStorage and localStorage. Values restore before mount hooks. Assignment writes a JSON-compatible value, bounded to 64 KiB; nested object mutations need reassignment. Template handlers rerender after completing; background changes call await this.tac.render(). Denied storage, malformed values and quota errors leave the UI usable. Do not store secrets in these fields.

sections.heading: Cached reads
sections.body: this.tac.fetch is network-first by default. Its optional IndexedDB cache accepts only same-origin GET/HEAD requests with credentials: 'omit' and no Authorization header. Private, no-store and Vary responses are excluded. cache: 'cache-first' explicitly permits a stored response to answer first; cache: 'no-store' bypasses persistence. Responses and storage are bounded, and cache failure falls back to ordinary fetching. This is not a client database or a server-table mirror.

sections.heading: Topics
sections.body:
A topic is an append-only log under `.tachyon/topics`, served as server-sent events from `/.tachyon/topics/<name>`. A subscriber holds the stream open and resumes from its last position, so a browser that was away replays what it missed rather than losing it. A log is read up to 16 MiB in one pass and polled for new records.

A route that streams its own values is a different thing — that is `@Stream` on a handler, under Yon.

sections.heading: Signals between components
sections.body: A document-scoped publish and subscribe bus carries values between components that have no parent in common. `@publish` on a field sends its value under a name, `@subscribe` receives it, and the bus retains the last value so a component that mounts later is not left waiting for the next one. One failing subscriber does not stop the others.

cookbook.title: Cookbook
cookbook.summary: Concrete recipes for building Tachyon apps without leaving the frontend-first workflow. This website is frontend-only, so these patterns can be explored with Tac companions before a Yon server exists.

sections.heading: Frontend-only prototype
sections.body: Start with client/ only. Tac renders pages and components, and companions provide the reactive UI controller. When you later add server/routes, the UI contract can stay the same.
sections.code:
client/
  pages/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.html
  components/panel/users/tac.js
  shared/data/docs.json

sections.heading: Signal-driven UI
sections.body: Publish and subscribe decorators replace manual event wiring between companion scripts. A form can publish a collection change and every interested panel can refresh itself without knowing who sent the signal.

sections.heading: Polyglot middleware boundary
sections.body: A `middleware.<ext>` at the project root is consulted before every request and after every response. It answers `before` and `after` rather than an HTTP method, so it speaks the protocol itself — JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and PHP. The compiled languages are not supported for middleware, because the protocol runtime appended to a compiled handler dispatches on the HTTP method and would find neither phase.

sections.heading: Native target polish
sections.body: Keep the shared HTML and responsive styles, then add platform behavior in the page companion. Native hosts set a document marker; a stylesheet can use it without depending on nonexistent template globals. Use a target-native companion for OS SDK calls and explicitly handle its asynchronous results.

operations.title: Operations
operations.summary: Health and readiness endpoints, generated OpenAPI docs, middleware hooks, rate limiting, and OpenTelemetry spans come built in.

sections.heading: Observability
sections.body: Every request carries a correlation identifier, generated in-process and threaded through the handler protocol, so a request and the handler invocation it caused can be tied together in a log. Failures arrive as Diagnostics v1 with stable codes — the same structure a build emits — and `--diagnostic-format json` makes them machine-readable. Tracing exporters are not built in.
sections.code:
ty preview --diagnostic-format json
ty doctor            # toolchains and handler runtimes

sections.heading: Build and deploy
sections.body: ty bundle writes dist/web by default. Use --target all during release validation, then preview or package the individual target you intend to ship.
sections.code:
ty bundle --target all
ty preview --target web
ty preview --target macos

sections.heading: Security
sections.body:
Every response carries defensive headers, and a strict content security policy is one of them — `script-src 'self'`, no inline script, `object-src 'none'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`. A handler runs as one bounded process with a deadline and a concurrency limit, its frames are bounded at 16 MiB, and a declared route contract is validated by CHEX before the handler is called at all.

There is no built-in authentication and no CORS layer. Both belong to the application: a middleware answers `before` every request, which is where a policy of either kind goes.
sections.code:
cache-control: no-store
referrer-policy: no-referrer
x-frame-options: DENY
x-content-type-options: nosniff
content-security-policy: default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  img-src 'self' data:; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'
  'inline-speculation-rules'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none'

platform-apis.title: Platform APIs
platform-apis.summary: A page in a browser is a page: it uses the web platform directly. A page in a native host is the same page, in the platform's own WebView, with a small shim around it — and a compiled companion beside it that reaches the platform's SDK because it was compiled as that language for that target.

sections.heading: There is no capability vocabulary
sections.body:
Tachyon does not put a list of verbs between an application and its platform. A tray, a notification, a file dialog — those are the platform's, and a companion written in the platform's own language already has them. A fixed list in the middle could only ever be the subset Tachyon had got round to implementing, in three hosts, for every platform at once, and an application would be stuck behind whatever that subset happened to be.

So the browser half uses web APIs, and the native half uses AppKit, UIKit, the Android framework or Win32 — each from the language that already speaks it.

sections.heading: What the host injects
sections.body:
Three things, and deliberately no more. The document body carries `data-platform="native"`, so a page can style or behave differently without sniffing a user agent. `tachyonWindow` carries the window controls the manifest granted. And the companion channel runs in both directions — a companion publishes to the page, and the page invokes the companion.

The publish stub queues rather than delivers: a companion may publish from a thread of its own before the page's modules have run, and without the queue that value is lost to a race nothing in the application can see.

sections.heading: Window controls are granted, not assumed
sections.body: manifest.json declares the window a native target opens and the controls a page may request, under a tachyon member a browser ignores. Nothing is granted by default. Ungranted controls are not exposed to the page, and the host checks the manifest grants before carrying out a request. Test for an exposed tachyonWindow function before using it. These controls do not sandbox application-owned native companion code, which runs with the host process's OS privileges.

sections.heading: Portable companion spelling
sections.body: A companion is written in its own language and reaches its own platform directly, so there is no portable verb list to learn. What is shared is the shape: a class whose fields are state and whose methods are behaviour, the two persistence lifetimes the browser gives a page, and `tacPublish` to send a value back. Each language spells those the way it spells everything else.

sections.heading: What the host records
sections.body: A packaged host writes `tachyon.host.json` beside its bundle, naming the target it was built for and the one capability the bridge offers: `companion.invoke`. It is one line because there is one thing to say — everything else an application reaches, it reaches through its own language.
sections.code: { "hostCapabilities": ["companion.invoke"] }
